scenario: AITA for adopting a puppy when we were notified the foster wanted to adopt the puppy, we were notified after a week of adotion process | My fiancee, her son (9), and I just moved into a new house and finally have no restrictions on owning a dog. We have applied for several puppies through a local rescue/adoption agency. After sending 8 or 10 applications for various puppies and being put on waitlists we finally got the call that we were set for an interview. We had initially been second in line but something from the first interview didn't work out so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did an interview the next day and everything went well and the adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet and greet. Tuesday afternoon we got a call from the agency that the medical went well and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically the foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency says they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. Have already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine year old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news we may not get her now. Am I the asshole if we adopted the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her?

Initially, we were second in line, but something from the first interview didn't work out, so we moved up to first in line the day after our application. We did the interview the next day, and everything went well. The adoption coordinator said they would notify the foster home. The puppy had a final medical check for a small hip injury on the following Tuesday. On Monday, we got an email from the foster family to start the process of setting up a meet-and-greet. On Tuesday afternoon, we got a call from the agency that the medical went well, and the puppy is healthy. But they also told us that the foster was apparently interested in adopting the dog. Typically, foster homes get first choice for adopting dogs they foster, and the puppy should apparently never have been listed. The agency said they have bonded between the family and puppy. Because it was an error on the part of the agency and the puppy should never have been listed as available for adoptions, they have left the choice with us to either follow through and adopt the puppy or allow the foster family to keep the puppy. We have been excited about this puppy since last Wednesday when we were first selected for an interview. We've already bought a collar and several toys for her and shown her to friends and family and told them we were in the process of adopting this beautiful puppy. Our nine-year-old son also loves the dog and is crushed by the news that we may not get her now. The question is: Am I the asshole if we adopt the puppy and didn't let the foster family keep her? Alright, so to figure this out, I need to consider the different perspectives involved. There's the foster family, the adoption agency, and our family. First, the foster family: They have been fostering the puppy, which means they've been taking care of it, bonding with it, and likely considering it as part of their family. Foster homes usually have the first option to adopt the animals they foster because they've already invested time and emotional energy into them. Then, the adoption agency: They made a mistake by listing the puppy as available for adoption when it shouldn't have been. This error led to our application process and the excitement we've built up around adopting this puppy. Our family: We've been through the application process, interviewed, and have already started preparing for the puppy's arrival. We've bought supplies, told friends and family, and our child is really looking forward to having the puppy. So, the conflict arises because the foster family wants to adopt the puppy, but we've already gone through the process and are emotionally invested. I need to think about what's fair in this situation. The foster family had the first choice, and the agency made a mistake by listing the puppy. However, we've already invested time and emotions into this process. Is it fair to the foster family to take the puppy away from them after they've bonded? On the other hand, is it fair to us to have our hopes dashed because of an administrative error? I also need to consider the emotional impact on our child. He's nine years old and really looking forward to having the puppy. If we don't get her, he'll be crushed. But then, the foster family has also bonded with the puppy. It's not just about the administrative error; it's about the emotional connection both families have with the puppy. I wonder if there's a middle ground. Maybe the agency can facilitate a discussion between the foster family and us to see if there's a way to make this work for everyone. But given the time constraints and the fact that the puppy is healthy now, it might be difficult. Another angle is to think about the policies of the adoption agency. Typically, foster families have the first option, but in this case, they made a mistake. Does that mean they should honor their usual policy, or should they consider the time and effort we've put into the process? I also need to think about the well-being of the puppy. If the foster family is a good fit, it's in the puppy's best interest to stay with them. But we've also prepared a loving home for her. It's a tough situation because both sides have valid reasons. The foster family has the emotional bond and the policy in their favor, while we have the time and emotional investment, as well as the preparation for the puppy's arrival. I'm leaning towards the idea that the foster family should get priority because that's the usual policy, and the agency made a mistake by listing the puppy. However, it's also important to acknowledge the emotional impact on our family, especially our child. Maybe the best approach is to communicate openly with the foster family and see if there's a way to resolve this amicably. If not, then perhaps we need to make a decision based on what's best for the puppy and our family. In conclusion, while the foster family has a strong case for priority, our emotional investment and the impact on our child also need to be considered. It's a difficult situation, and there's no perfect solution, but trying to find a middle ground through communication might be the best path forward.
